name: Poisoning the well
statement: Discrediting a source in advance lowers belief in whatever it says next, from 5.86 to 4.60 on a 0 to 10 scale, a discount rather than the dismissal the name implies.
meaning: The move is to attack a speaker before the speaker argues, so that the argument arrives already suspect. Textbooks file it under ad hominem and separate it by timing: the personal attack comes first, and it is aimed at everything the target has not yet said. Walton argues the split is not about timing at all. On his account the fallacy is dialectical, a tactic at the confrontation stage of a discussion that removes the other side's standing to make any move, and it resists analysis by the ad hominem argument schemes. The atlas covers the after-the-fact version under ad hominem, where the experimental record is much thicker, and covers the effect of a named source on the same message under source bias. What is left to this entry is the timing, and the timing turns out to be the part almost nobody has measured. Two literatures come close. Forewarning research warns people that a persuasive appeal is coming, which is not the same manipulation, because it discredits an intent rather than a person. Sleeper-effect research places a discounting cue before or after the arguments and reads persuasion off both, which is the same manipulation asked a different question. Neither was designed to test the fallacy, and both contradict the confident version of it.

origin.note: Newman was answering Charles Kingsley, who had written in a review of Froude in Macmillan's Magazine for January 1864, pages 216 and 217, signed 'C. K.', that 'Truth, for its own sake, had never been a virtue with the Roman clergy'. Kingsley's follow-up pamphlet said he was 'henceforth in doubt and fear, as much as any honest man can be, concerning every word Dr. Newman may write'. Newman's reply, published as a pamphlet on Thursday 21 April 1864, calls that 'this unmanly attempt of his, in his concluding pages, to cut the ground from under my feet;-to poison by anticipation the public mind against me', and then 'This I call poisoning the wells'. Both passages were read in the 1864 text at the Newman Reader, which marks Part 1 as not reprinted in 1865, and again in the Preface to the 1865 edition, which carries the same wording with Kingsley's name removed. Newman writes 'as I may call it' and 'This I call', which is the phrasing of someone applying a metaphor rather than reporting a term already in use. No earlier use of the phrase in an argumentative sense was located; the search covered Crossref by title, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on fallacies, which does not contain the word poison, and general web search.

evidence:
The only located study that isolates the timing is Thalhofer and Kirscht, in Psychological Reports in 1968. Its abstract, read at Crossref, reports that source derogation cut persuasion on contested issues only where the source was already rated unfavourably, and that 'Time of source derogation was important; source derogation before issue support reduced persuasiveness while derogation after support did not'. The full text was not obtained, so no sample size, effect size or interval from it appears here.

The closest modern measurement of the structure comes from Ecker and colleagues, who tested source discreditation as a way of countering misinformation. Experiment 1 gave 292 Prolific participants five fictional news reports in five within-subject versions. Reliance on the misinformation, scored 0 to 10, was 6.87 with no intervention, 5.17 after the source was discredited for a conflict of interest, 4.62 after the claim itself was corrected, 4.17 after both, and 4.11 in a version that never carried the misinformation. Discrediting the source worked, F(1, 291) = 110.07, eta p squared = .274, p < .001, and worked less well than correcting the claim, F(1, 291) = 9.61, eta p squared = .032, p = .002. Experiment 2 ran 564 participants and added the measure that matches the fallacy. Of three claims the source had not made, participants were asked, 'If SOURCE were to make the following claim, to what extent would you believe it?' For a person source, belief in those future claims fell from 5.86 with no discredit to 4.60 after a conflict-of-interest discredit, and to 4.10 after a poor-track-record one. For a media outlet the figures were 5.89, 4.70 and 4.63. The main effect of condition was F(3, 1686) = 100.74, p < .001, eta p squared = .152. Perceived credibility of the source fell further than belief in its future claims did, from 6.56 to 4.26 and 3.59 for the person source.

Pratkanis, Greenwald, Leippe and Baumgardner ran the cue-placement manipulation 29 times across 17 experiments. Their cue is a discredit, either a low-credibility source or an editor's note declaring the article false, and their question is what happens to persuasion over weeks. Fourteen treatments across Experiments 1 to 12 and 17 put the discredit before the message, and none of them produced a reliable delayed rise in agreement. Experiment 7 separated source from message by two intervening items. A low-credibility source named before the message was followed by a fall in agreement across the delay, F(1, 22) = 10.80, p < .01. The same source named two items afterwards was followed by a rise, F(1, 22) = 12.16, p < .01. Experiment 17 recruited 400 students and reached 294 of them by telephone six weeks later. On a source-credibility scale running from -40 to +40, readers who met the discrediting note before the article rated the source at 6.04, those who met it afterwards at 2.88, and those who read the article with a neutral note at 14.65. Immediate opinion in the cue-after conditions sat near the no-message control and then rose, F(1, 114) = 8.40, p < .01, while the cue-before condition produced moderate immediate movement that did not decay, F(1, 127) = 1.15. Six weeks on, 8.4% of participants could say what the note had said.

Kumkale and Albarracín pooled 72 data sets on discounting cues. In 53% the cue came before the message and in 39% after. Their Table 3 asks whether a discredited message backfires, and it does not. Immediately after exposure, people who got the message with a discounting cue agreed with it more than people given no message at all, d+ = 0.19, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.28, k = 26, N = 1,547. At the delayed test the gap was d+ = 0.30, CI 0.20 to 0.40, k = 22, N = 1,535. The source-bias entry carries the rest of that meta-analysis.

Wood and Quinn synthesised forewarning twice, and the warning there is about an incoming appeal rather than about a person. Measured before the appeal arrived, warnings moved people towards the position the appeal was going to take, d = 0.37, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.46, k = 20. Warnings that named an intent to persuade moved them further, d = 0.42, CI 0.30 to 0.54, k = 8, than warnings naming only topic and stance, d = 0.22, CI 0.07 to 0.36, k = 8, QB(1) = 4.54, p < .05. That reversed where the topic mattered to the audience. Within the three studies that varied it, involving topics gave d = -0.31, CI -0.61 to -0.02, against 0.07, CI -0.13 to 0.27, for uninvolving ones, QB(1) = 4.60, p < .05. Measured after the appeal had been delivered, warned recipients resisted, d = -0.38, CI -0.48 to -0.27, k = 17. Involvement again dominated, -0.92, CI -1.22 to -0.63, against -0.01, CI -0.25 to 0.23, k = 6 each, QB(1) = 22.08, p < .001.

replication.headline: No experiment on poisoning the well by that name was located. Where the timing has been isolated the results disagree: a 1968 study found a discredit before the message cut persuasion and one after it did not, and Pratkanis's 17 experiments found the opposite ordering on immediate opinion, with the pre-emptive discredit leaving more agreement in place than the late one.
replication.detail:
The component claim, that discrediting a source lowers uptake of what it says, is repeated and holds. Ecker's Experiment 2 reproduced Experiment 1's discreditation effect in a larger and differently designed sample, 564 against 292, and extended it to claims the source had not yet made. The claim that the pre-emptive version is the damaging one is where the record splits. Thalhofer and Kirscht report that derogation before the argument reduced persuasion and derogation after did not. Pratkanis and colleagues, manipulating the same variable 29 times, found that a discredit arriving after the arguments suppressed immediate agreement to the level of people who had read nothing, while a discredit arriving first left moderate agreement standing. The two are not measuring quite the same thing, since the 1968 study reports persuasion at one time point and the 1988 series reports the whole persistence curve, and no study located here runs the two orderings against each other on a modern measure. Ecker and colleagues say as much about their own materials, writing that future work could compare concurrent with retrospective presentation in the same study.

The claim that a poisoned well leaves nothing drinkable fails on every measure located. Pooled over 26 data sets, people who received a message alongside a discounting cue still moved towards it relative to people given no message, d+ = 0.19. In Ecker's Experiment 2 the discredited source's future claims were still believed at 4.10 to 4.70 on a 0 to 10 scale. Pratkanis's participants forgot the discredit before they forgot the argument, with 8.4% able to restate the note after six weeks. The searches behind this verdict ran over Crossref by title and by DOI, PubMed, PMC, Europe PMC by way of publisher pages, the Springer pages for Argumentation and Law and Human Behavior, and general web search, pairing poisoning the well with experiment, participants, persuasion and replication.

study.cite: Pratkanis, A. R., Greenwald, A. G., Leippe, M. R., & Baumgardner, M. H. (1988). In search of reliable persuasion effects: III. The sleeper effect is dead. Long live the sleeper effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(2), 203-218. Twenty-nine tests across 17 experiments, with the discrediting cue placed before or after the message.

limits:
The manipulations quoted here are not the fallacy. Wood and Quinn's warnings announce that an appeal is coming and sometimes that it means to persuade, which discredits an intention rather than a person, and their own moderator analysis found resistance whether or not intent was named. Pratkanis's Experiment 17 cue is an editor's note saying the article's conclusion is false, which attacks the claim rather than the writer; the source-credibility manipulation runs through Experiments 1 to 12 instead. Ecker's discreditation is delivered after the misinformation, and only its new-claim measure has the pre-emptive shape.

Four documents were not obtained. Thalhofer and Kirscht is quoted only from the abstract at Crossref, so its design, its sample and the size of its timing effect are unknown here. Walton's 2006 paper is paywalled at Springer and is quoted from its abstract. Almagro Holgado and Haro Marchal's 2025 reply is paywalled at the same publisher and is quoted from its abstract. Steblay, Hosch, Culhane and McWethy's meta-analysis of judicial instructions to disregard, 175 hypothesis tests from 48 studies with 8,474 participants, was read only at its PubMed abstract, which carries no effect size. It is a neighbouring phenomenon in any case, measuring what jurors do with evidence they have already heard and been told to set aside.

No structured effect size is given. The candidates measure different things, a longitudinal slope in Pratkanis, a within-study attitude shift in Wood and Quinn, a difference from a no-message baseline in Kumkale and Albarracín and a rating on an eleven-point scale in Ecker, and pairing any two of them as original and replication would invent a comparison none of them makes. Pratkanis's d values in Table 1 are slopes of the persistence function divided by the standard deviation of the slope, not standardised mean differences, and they are not comparable with the others.

Samples are narrow. Pratkanis used students, and his computerised experiments ran 12 to 60 participants per test. Wood and Quinn's premessage synthesis rests on 20 study outcomes, and its involvement comparison on three studies each side. Ecker's participants were Prolific panellists reading fictional news about invented drugs and bands, chosen so that political priors would not intrude, which is also the condition under which a real pre-emptive attack would matter most.
misreadings:
The largest error is treating every advance warning about a source as the fallacy. Almagro Holgado and Haro Marchal argue against what they call the neutral view, on which poisoning the well silences a speaker on the basis of social identity and can never be legitimate, and their abstract ends 'Poisoning the well is, many times, a virtuous move'. The applied literature agrees from the other direction: Ecker and colleagues tested discrediting a source as a recommended countermeasure to misinformation and found it works, which makes telling an audience in advance that a source has a conflict of interest a public-health intervention rather than a trick. Whether the move is fair turns on whether the discredit is true and bears on the premises the audience is being asked to accept, which is the test the ad hominem entry sets out from Bondy.

The second error is reading the metaphor literally. A poisoned well is undrinkable, and a discredited source is discounted. People who read a message with a discounting cue still shifted towards it, d+ = 0.19 against no message at all. Ecker's participants put belief in the discredited source's future claims at 4.10 to 4.70 out of 10 rather than at zero.

The third is assuming the pre-emptive attack must beat the late one because it arrives first. That prediction has been isolated twice and answered twice, in opposite directions, and one of those answers comes from an abstract. Where the whole time course is available, the pre-emptive discredit is the durable one and the late discredit is the one that wears off, which is a different claim from the one the fallacy makes.

A fourth is expecting a warning to produce resistance. Wood and Quinn found that warnings delivered before an appeal moved people towards it, and moved them further when the warning said the appeal meant to persuade. Resistance appeared once the topic mattered to the audience, or once the appeal had actually been read. Ordinary primacy is also a poor guide here, since the serial-position work in the recency entry concerns recall of list items rather than the weight given to an argument.

Part 1, Mr. Kingsley's Method of Disputation, published as a pamphlet on 21 April 1864. The phrases 'to poison the wells', 'to poison by anticipation the public mind against me' and 'This I call poisoning the wells' were read in this text.
Newman, J. H. (1865). Apologia Pro Vita Sua, Preface to the 1865 edition. The same passage, carried over from the 1864 pamphlet with Kingsley named as 'my Accuser'.

Kingsley, C. (1864). Extract from a review of Froude's History of England, Macmillan's Magazine for January 1864, pages 216 to 217, signed 'C. K.', and 'What, Then, Does Dr. Newman Mean?', third edition. Source of the sentence Newman answered and of the closing passage he called poisoning the wells.

Thalhofer, N. N., & Kirscht, J. P. (1968). Source Derogation and Persuasion on Controverted Issues. Psychological Reports, 23(3 suppl), 1179-1184. Full text not obtained; the timing finding is quoted from the abstract at Crossref.

Ecker, U. K. H., Prike, T., Paver, A. B., Scott, R. J., & Swire-Thompson, B. (2024). Don't believe them! Reducing misinformation influence through source discreditation. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 9, 52. Read as the full text at PMC; both experiments and the new-claim measure are taken from it.

Pratkanis, A. R., Greenwald, A. G., Leippe, M. R., & Baumgardner, M. H. (1988). In search of reliable persuasion effects: III. The sleeper effect is dead. Long live the sleeper effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(2), 203-218. Read as the PDF hosted by the third author; the cue-placement counts, Experiment 7 and Experiment 17 are taken from the article text and Table 1.

Kumkale, G. T., & Albarracín, D. (2004). The sleeper effect in persuasion: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 130(1), 143-172. Read as the PDF hosted by the second author's laboratory; the cue-placement percentages and Table 3 are taken from the document text.

Wood, W., & Quinn, J. M. (2003). Forewarned and forearmed? Two meta-analytic syntheses of forewarnings of influence appeals. Psychological Bulletin, 129(1), 119-138. Read as the PDF hosted by the first author; all figures re-extracted from the document text.

Walton, D. N. (2006). Poisoning the Well. Argumentation, 20(3), 273-307. Paywalled at Springer; the account of the fallacy as dialectical rather than a species of ad hominem is quoted from the abstract.

Almagro Holgado, M., & Haro Marchal, A. (2025). Against the Neutral View of Poisoning the Well. Argumentation, 39(1), 129-146. Paywalled at Springer; the argument that many instances are legitimate is quoted from the abstract.

Law and Human Behavior, 30(4), 469-492. Read only at the PubMed abstract, which reports 175 hypothesis tests from 48 studies with 8,474 participants and no effect size. Cited as a neighbouring phenomenon.

Hansen, H. (2024). Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Checked for the term; the entry does not contain the word poison, which is why the origin note reports where the search for an earlier use looked.
